We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts list. Need number of methyl groups (CH3). Methyl carbons appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, also maybe 20-30. In list we have 26.40, 36.40 (two identical), 58.70, plus aromatic carbons (130-168). The methyl likely at 26.40 ppm. 36.40 could be methylene or tertiary carbon. 58.70 likely carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3). Could be methoxy carbon (O-CH3) also appears ~55 ppm. That is also a methyl group (OCH3). So there may be two methyl groups: one aliphatic (26.4) and one methoxy (58.7). Need to infer molecular structure? Could also be a carbonyl carbon at 168.30 (C=O). Aromatics 130-124. So maybe compound is anisole derivative with carbonyl? For example, methyl benzoate? Methyl benzoate has carbonyl carbon ~166, aromatic ~130-128, OCH3 carbon ~52, and carbonyl carbon attached to OCH3. It also has a carbonyl carbon (C=O) and aromatic carbons. Methyl benzoate has one methyl (the OCH3). No aliphatic methyl at 26. So 26.4 maybe a methyl attached to aromatic (toluene). Could be p-methyl anisole? That would have two methyls: one OCH3 (~55) and one aromatic CH3 (~21). But 26.4 is a bit higher. Could be a carbon attached to carbonyl (acetyl) CH3 at ~26. So maybe compound is acetophenone (methyl phenyl ketone). That has carbonyl carbon ~200, aromatic, methyl carbon ~30. But we have carbonyl at 168 (maybe ester). So maybe methyl acetate? Not aromatic. Hmm.

We have two identical 36.40 signals, maybe two equivalent carbons (CH2). Could be a cyclohexyl? Not sure.

But question: "How many methyl (CH3) groups are present in the sample's molecule?" We need to deduce from NMR data. Methyl carbons appear as distinct signals. We have at least two possible methyl signals: 26.40 and 58.70. 36.40 likely not methyl (more like CH2). So answer likely 2.

Let's verify by retrieving typical carbon shift ranges for methyl groups.
